before_step.derivation: From step 1, a path is a length-18 string s=s_1...s_18 over {R,D} with nine R and nine D, and position k records the k-th move. Define prefix counts R(k)=# of R among s_1..s_k and D(k)=# of D among s_1..s_k, so R(k)+D(k)=k and each position k of the path is (R(k),D(k)). The path visits cell (a,b) precisely when, for some k with 0<=k<=18, R(k)=a and D(k)=b; since a+b=k, this is equivalent to the prefix ending at position a+b having exactly a R moves (and hence b D moves). Because moves are monotone, no cell is visited twice, but a cell is visited at all exactly when that count-prefix (a,b) occurs. Therefore the constraint 'do not visit cell (a,b)' forbids exactly those strings having a prefix of length a+b in which the number of R moves is a (equivalently, the prefix is a string over {R,D} with a R's and b D's, followed by the remaining 18-(a+b) characters). Applying this to each listed forbidden cell gives five separate exclusion conditions: for (2,2), no prefix of length 4 has two R; for (4,3), no prefix of length 7 has four R; for (5,6), no prefix of length 11 has five R; for (7,5), no prefix of length 12 has seven R; for (8,8), no prefix of length 16 has eight R. Equivalently, each forbidden cell (a,b) excludes strings for which R(a+b)=a. A valid string must avoid all five, and the excluded sets may overlap; the condition is a set of prefix-count exclusions on the step-1 universe, independent of steps 2 and 4.
before_step.result: For each forbidden cell (a,b), a string is excluded iff some prefix has length a+b with exactly a R moves (hence b D moves), i.e. the count-prefix (a,b) occurs. Concretely, forbid prefixes (2,2),(4,3),(5,6),(7,5),(8,8): no prefix of length 4 with two R; length 7 with four R; length 11 with five R; length 12 with seven R; length 16 with eight R.

plan_step.goal: Translate each forbidden cell (a,b) into a prefix condition: after k moves #R=a and #D=b; exclude strings whose prefixes reach those counts.

The path is at (R(k),D(k)) after k moves, since R increases x by 1 and D increases y by 1. Thus the path visits cell (a,b) exactly when some k satisfies R(k)=a and D(k)=b. Because R(k)+D(k)=k, this can only happen at k=a+b, so visiting (a,b) is equivalent to the prefix of length a+b having exactly a R moves. Since the prefix length is a+b, having a R moves also means having (a+b)-a=b D moves. Conversely, if the prefix of length a+b has a R moves and b D moves, then after those a+b moves the path is at (a,b). Therefore forbidding a visit to (a,b) is exactly forbidding strings whose prefix of length a+b contains a R moves, equivalently whose count-prefix (a,b) occurs. Applying this to the five forbidden cells gives: (2,2) forbids prefix length 4 with 2 R; (4,3) forbids prefix length 7 with 4 R; (5,6) forbids prefix length 11 with 5 R; (7,5) forbids prefix length 12 with 7 R; (8,8) forbids prefix length 16 with 8 R. A valid string must avoid all five prefix-count conditions. These exclusions are independent of the no-RRR/no-DDD condition and of the checkpoint condition.
